0LlTuo0LZoQJgMCDovNMwn.title: Largo [Harpsichord Concerto No. 5 in F minor BWV 1056]

s.t: Ward Swingle told soprano Christiane Legrand to imagine Miles Davis playing the melody; by displacing it and adding subtle embellishments, she turned The Swingle Singers’ Largo into a jazz ballad.
s.src: The Swingle Singers: Making the Music Dance (Jazz History Online, Thomas Cunniffe)
s.q: Swingle told Legrand to imagine Miles Davis playing Bach’s melody. By simply displacing the melody and adding subtle soloistic embellishments, Legrand transformed the piece into a touching jazz ballad.

s.t: Johann Sebastian Bach had already used it as a melancholy oboe solo opening his cantata ‘Ich steh mit einem Fuss im Grabe’ (‘I stand with one foot in the grave’).
s.src: Ich steh mit einem Fuss im Grabe, BWV 156 (Netherlands Bach Society)
s.q: The six-part cantata ‘Ich steh mit einem Fuss im Grabe’ opens with a Sinfonia that is dominated by a melancholy oboe solo, which Bach was to reuse later in his harpsichord concerto BWV 1056 . … I stand with one foot in the grave

s.t: Joanna Forbes L’Estrange, later The Swingles’ musical director, said singing along to the Largo on her mum’s original Swingle Singers records was a childhood highlight.
s.q: My mum had a Jazz Sebastian Bach LP and many of the other original records; singing along to Largo was a highlight for me, whenever I used to go and visit her as a child. … When I became the Swingles MD in 1999

s.t: The Swingle Singers’ recording of this Largo was used in the 2023 film Beau Is Afraid.
s.src: Swingle Singers recordings featured in films and ads (Swingle Music)
s.q: 2023 film beau is afraid In this film the recording of Largo [Harpsichord Concerto No. 5 in F minor BWV 1056] was used.

f.t: They began as Paris session singers who, wanting a greater challenge than singing ‘ooh’ and ‘ah’ behind Charles Aznavour and Édith Piaf, sight-sang through Johann Sebastian Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier.
f.src: The Swingle Singers: Making the Music Dance (Jazz History Online, Thomas Cunniffe)
f.q: In mid-1962, Swingle and seven other vocalists gathered to sight-sing through Bach’s “ Well-Tempered Clavier ”. All of the singers were instrumentalists as well as vocalists, and they were looking for a musical challenge greater than singing “ooh” and “ah” behind Charles Aznavour and Edith Piaf .

f.t: Their first US tour clashed with Les Double Six’s North American tour, so its leader Mimi Perrin had to recruit new singers to replace those away singing with them.
f.src: The Swingle Singers: Making the Music Dance (Jazz History Online, Thomas Cunniffe)
f.q: the Swingle Singers made their first US tour (Ironically, the Double Six toured North America at the same time, and Perrin had to recruit new vocalists to replace those performing with the Swingle Singers)

f.t: Their scat syllables were mostly never written down: Ward Swingle’s arrangements left them out, so they sang whichever syllables the members found easiest.
f.src: The Swingle Singers: Making the Music Dance (Jazz History Online, Thomas Cunniffe)
f.q: In fact, Swingle’s original arrangements did not have most of the scat syllables written in, and the eventual syllables used were those that the members found easiest to sing.

f.t: Their first album was meant to be sold to family and friends, yet its American success took them to the White House to sing for President and Mrs Johnson.
f.src: The Swingle Singers: Making the Music Dance (Jazz History Online, Thomas Cunniffe)
f.q: Swingle approached Pierre Fatosme of Philips Records with the thought of making a “jazz Bach” record that they might sell to family and friends. … a concert for President and Mrs. Johnson at the White House.

f.t: Luciano Berio wrote their eight amplified voices into his Sinfonia for the New York Philharmonic; Ward Swingle estimated they performed it about 200 times.
f.src: The Swingle Singers: Making the Music Dance (Jazz History Online, Thomas Cunniffe)
f.q: Commissioned by the New York Philharmonic for its 125th anniversary, the work calls for a very large orchestra and the eight amplified voices of the Swingle Singers. … (Ward Swingle estimates that the Swingle Singers have done about 200 performances of the piece since its premiere)

nf.t: Its soprano’s brief: imagine Miles Davis playing Bach’s melody, and sing it that way
nf.src: The Swingle Singers: Making the Music Dance (Jazz History Online, Thomas Cunniffe)
